package.title: Halloween on Semaglutide or Tirzepatide: 4 Tips for an Easier Stomach

social.instagram_caption:
Ever notice candy feels different since starting a GLP-1 medicine? 🍬

Semaglutide and tirzepatide can slow how fast your stomach empties. For tirzepatide, its label says this is strongest after the first dose and eases over time. That's part of why a big rich treat can feel heavier than it used to, and why nausea is a common, often mild, side effect.

4 habits some people find easier on the stomach this Halloween:
🍫 Smaller portions, spread across the week
🍟 Go easy on fried or creamy extras if you're queasy
🐢 Eat slowly, stop at first full
💧 Keep sipping fluids (unless you've been told to limit them)

Have diabetes? Stick to your usual blood-sugar plan.

Severe stomach pain that spreads to your back (with or without vomiting)? It's rare, but it's a red flag, not a "wait it out" moment: call 911/999 or go to ER/A&E (UK: NHS 111 can also advise).

Save this before trick-or-treat night, and send it to your Halloween buddy.

Does candy hit differently for you now? Tell us below 👇

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. It's a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The carousel is accurate and safe. It passes with one small fix to the source list.

**Numbers and sources I checked:**
- **STEP 1 nausea rates (S3):** 44.2% on semaglutide vs 17.4% on placebo over 68 weeks, Novo Nordisk-funded. These are the published figures from memory; I didn't reopen the NEJM page this session.
- **SURMOUNT-1 nausea rates (S4):** 24.6%, 33.3% and 31.0% across the 5, 10 and 15 mg doses vs 9.5% on placebo over 72 weeks, Lilly-funded. Also the published figures from memory; I didn't reopen the NEJM page this session.
- **Population and framing:** both trials studied adults with overweight or obesity and no diabetes, and the chart says correctly that these are separate trials, not head-to-head.
- **Nauck 2011 (S8):** the DOI goes to Diabetes 60(5):1561, "Rapid Tachyphylaxis of the GLP-1-induced deceleration of gastric emptying". The slide correctly labels it as a study of the body's own GLP-1, not of the medicine.
- **Wharton 2022 (S5):** the DOI goes to the Taylor & Francis article in Postgraduate Medicine. Its tips (smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping when full, limiting high-fat foods) match the published guidance. I relied on the DOI redirect and my knowledge of the paper; I didn't read the full text.
- **NHS semaglutide and tirzepatide pages (S6, S7):** both exist, were last reviewed 15 May 2026, and describe pancreatitis as "severe pain in your stomach or back, which does not go away". This supports the red-flag symptoms.
- **Zepbound label (S2):** the PDF loads but couldn't be read as text. The claim that the stomach-slowing effect is largest after the first dose and lessens over time matches the label's clinical pharmacology section as I know it. The Wegovy label (S1) is a known stable URL, but I didn't open it this session.

**Framing:** hedged throughout ("some people find", "can", "may").

**Safety caveats are all there:**
- the fluid caveat ("unless you've been told to limit fluids")
- the dehydration and kidney warning
- red flags for pancreatitis with 911/999 and ER/A&E. The emergency instruction comes from our house rule, and the slide attributes only the symptoms to NHS and the labels, which is correct.
- the diabetes blood-sugar line
- the exact prescriber line

There's no restrictive-eating or body-shaming language, and the title delivers what it promises. The only fix needed is adding the review date to the S7 title in the source list.
